Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette: The firefight had erupted without warning, and above the shouting, a transport helicopter had fought to stay aloft, its engines whining in a pitch that now lived permanently in Kwame's nervous system. Whenever he recalled that day, the memory arrived with startling clarity, each detail sharp and more real than any ordinary recollection. The scent of scorched earth and diesel would flood his senses the moment his mind wandered back, pulling him out of the present. The relentless clarity of those memories convinced him that he had been permanently changed for the worse, cementing a paralyzing belief that he would never forgive himself for standing still when others were falling. Now working as a park ranger in the Pacific Northwest, Kwame found that the sound of a distant aircraft or a sudden mechanical noise immediately dialed his system into overdrive. The auditory trigger did not merely startle him; it actively shifted his baseline, forcing him to become hyper-vigilant and scan the tree line for invisible threats. As his alertness spiked, a strange, heavy discomfort would pool in his chest, and he would begin to feel detached from the trail beneath his boots, as though watching his own life through thick glass. What frightened him most was that growing sense of unreality, which reinforced his worst fears and made him certain that his mind was fracturing under the strain, deepening the conviction that he had been irrevocably damaged. This cycle quickly tightened into a rigid pattern. His conviction that he had to be on guard all the time actively pulled the combat memories back into his awareness, ensuring they surfaced with relentless frequency. As that sense of inescapable self-recrimination deepened, it also heightened his physiological baseline, meaning that the initial discomfort of a trigger was no longer dismissed but was immediately amplified into a full threat response. His constant scanning of the perimeter and intense watching of his coworkers fed directly back into his recall system; the more rigorously he monitored for danger, the more the past invaded his present with vivid, more-real-than-normal detail. His sustained state of threat assessment also actively reinforced his worst judgments about himself, solidifying the belief that he had been permanently damaged and could never relax, while simultaneously making him acutely sensitive to ordinary machinery, meaning routine engine sounds were instantly registered as potent danger cues. His mounting anxiety continuously pushed him further into dissociation, leaving him trapped in a self-reinforcing loop of dread. Over several months, the avoidance behaviours took root in his daily routine. Kwame began steering clear of the northern ridge trails where helicopter traffic crossed, and he stopped patrolling at dusk, claiming a sudden shoulder injury that his wife, Elena, recognized as a flimsy cover. His constant watching at camp made him jumpy around his colleagues' casual conversations, and the emotional distance he kept to maintain his hyper-vigilance created a quiet chasm between him and his spouse. He had come to believe that his mind was fundamentally broken, and the exhaustion of carrying that guilt while navigating daily life finally pushed him to sit in a clinician's office. What he most hoped for was a way to quiet the alarms without forgetting who he was, though he remained terrified that stepping back from his constant watch would leave him vulnerable to another moment he could never forgive himself for surviving.
